June 21, 1984
Security Intelligence Service

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-9, and Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto, be read a third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is interesting to be returning to Bill C-9, the Bill which will establish a civilian security service, after the House has debated standards for the manufacture of the Canadian flag. That debate evoked a great deal of patriotism. I certainly enjoyed that debate. I do not express any shame in being a Canadian patriot. I remember being very pleased when I saw the Canadian flag unveiled for the first time. I think that it is very much as a patriot that I express shame at what is before us today in Bill C-9.
Yes, we do need a civilian security service. Canada is a middle power, not a major power in the world. Our security needs are not as great as some other countries, nevertheless they do exist and we require an appropriate service to deal with them. Our requirements for national security are not as great as those of the United States. Some of the remarks which I will make this afternoon will deal with our safeguards. The safeguards which are in this legislation are not as good as the American safeguards, even though our own security needs are not as important as those of a major power such as the United States.
I think it would be useful in addressing this issue to examine a bit of the history in order to realize how we came to be in the state which we are with regard to Bill C-9. It does bear some relevance to what is wrong with the Bill as it currently stands. We will all remember that it was in a criminal trial in 1976 that members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police security service were discovered to have been involved in criminal wrongdoings. In 1977 the McDonald Commission was established. It sat until 1980, and it reported in 1981. At that time it was extremely critical of the practices of the current RCMP Security Service. It reported evidence of criminal wrongdoing in four provinces, but there were prosecutions only in the province of Quebec. The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) has said that there will not be further prosecutions, and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has referred to disciplinary action to be taken against the culprits in question. But in fact we have not been advised of any specific disciplinary action which has been taken against any of them.
I do not want to agree with all of the provisions and recommendations of the McDonald Commission. In some places I would consider them too lax. Nevertheless, it did come
up with a number of safeguards which should be built into the legislation for a civilian security service, and most of these recommended safeguards have been ignored. We saw them ignored in Bill C-157, and they are still left out of the current legislation. It was in May, 1983, that Bill C-157, the predecessor to Bill C-9, was tabled. It was met with denunciations from provincial attorneys general, civil liberties organizations, church groups, and from all kinds of private citizens all across the country. My own Party strenuously opposed this legislation. I regret to say that the Conservatives were not quite as vigorous in their opposition. Some of those Hon. Members, indeed, thought that the safeguards in Bill C-157 were quite adequate and, indeed, it was a rather civil libertarian kind of Bill.
I am very pleased to see the Conservatives have come along and are now joining in very concerted opposition to this very drastic and draconian legislation.
A Senate committee was established to hold public hearings on the old Bill, C-157, last summer. I cannot say anything too good about Senate committees. My own Party would like to see the Senate abolished. Certainly most of us feel very strongly that there should not be an appointed Senate, that elected people should be the people to do this. Our own Members, of course, were not involved in the Senate committee hearings because we do not have members in the Senate. Nevertheless, even with this rather senatorial committee looking at this Bill and holding these hearings, it did come up with some recommendation for additional safeguards. You might say it is a body not known for vigorous stands on civil liberties, but nevertheless it did see the need for additional safeguards. I regret to say that the Government did not even act on the advice of the Senate which is, by and large, appointed by the current Liberal Government.
Bill C-9 which is before us today is only very slightly changed from Bill C-157, and this whole process of consulting the public and holding hearings has really been a charade. In effect what Bill C-9 does is to make legal many of the activities which were condemned by the initial McDonald Commission and by the Canadian public. We had an example of wrongdoing, and what was done about it? Was it stopped? No, it is made legal. That is how we deal with wrongdoing on the part of the security service. We have 800,000 files opened against Canadian citizens. There is no way, Mr. Speaker, you can persuade anyone in this House that there are 800,000 terrorists or spies operating in Canada. We have a Government which has overreacted in how it has dealt with security matters in the past, and it has overreacted in trying to deal with security matters in the future by legislating a civilian security service with inadequate safeguards and far too many powers.
We are faced with the prospect of the opening of first class mail, wiretaps, doctors' and lawyers' records being invaded, people being bugged in their homes and offices, and all of this in the name of national security. Many of these activities certainly went on previously even though they were against the
June 21, 1984

law and we now have this very shameful approach, instead of stopping it, that it would be made lawful.
1 want to argue this afternoon basically three things which I believe are wrong with the Bill before us. First of all, the threats to security have been ill defined. They are far too broad. Second, the powers which have been given to the civilian security service are far too great. There is no proportion. It is given excessive powers even for dealing with quite trivial matters. Its excessive powers are not confined to major instances of threats to national security but can even be used for information gathering. Third, the accountability procedures are far too weak. They are thoroughly inadequate.
I would like to refer to a brief which has been submitted by a physician, Doctor Philip Berger, on the definition of "threats to security of Canada" from his experience. While this is an individual brief it does represent a considerable amount of opinion from a professional community. Doctor Berger reports that many physicians in Canada have examined and documented the cases of persons seeking refugee status in Canada who were tortured in their own home countries. The results of these investigations have been used to substantiate claims of torture for the classification of refugee status under the Immigration Act. They have also been used to expose human rights violations by foreign Governments.
This kind of activity can lead to a perfectly normal law-abiding physician being targeted, and the groups which are using the information obtained in these physical examinations could be targeted for intrusive surveillance. These physical examinations, medical examinations, have been used by groups within Canada who are opposed to totalitarian regimes. But some of these groups are perceived to advocate threats or use of acts of violence for the purpose of achieving a political objective within a foreign state. That brings it within the definition of a threat to security.
Some physicians are members of organizations which donate money to opposition groups in foreign states, who defend themselves in violent confrontations with their Governments. Clearly, these physicians are engaged in activities directed toward helping opposition groups trying to achieve a political objective within a foreign state. That makes them come under the definition of "threats to the security of Canada", preposterous as this may seem.
The Canadian Civil Liberties Association has noted a number of instances in which groups could be targeted for activities which, I believe, any normal person would consider quite appropriate, quite lawful and, indeed, quite laudable. There is within the Act a definition of activities directed towards certain types of security related misconduct. To what extent could this invite speculation about security threats which might happen at some indefinite point in the future? Consider, for example, the power the Bill would create for intrusive snooping into activities within Canada, directed toward or in support of acts of violence for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or foreign state?
This Section could mandate the use of bugging procedures, for example, or mail opening against a Canadian citizen, who,
Security Intelligence Service
without any foreign direction whatsoever, took up a collection for the State of Israel or the Palestinian Liberation Organization. Suppose such citizens got involved with rebels in El Salvador or even in Afghanistan and raised money for them? That certainly makes them liable to intrusive investigation.
Another Subsection would make intrusive surveillance available for activities intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow by violence of the constitutionally established system of government in Canada. What does "ultimate" mean? "Ultimate" is certainly a very long way away. It may have no immediate connection with any kind of violence or any kind of serious activity whatsoever. It is highly speculative that some activity carried on by what could be a perfectly lawful dissenting group could bring it under surveillance.
The Canadian Civil Liberties Association may draw inspiration, or may be seen to draw inspiration, from the American Civil Liberties Union. Does this mean that that organization is foreign influenced? What are the limits of detrimentals? Supposing a Canadian citizen were employed by a foreign corporation involved in commercial negotiations with the Canadian Government-obviously an activity which happens all the time-this would permit targeting of such an individual. Bill C-9 is a threat to law-abiding people and legitimate dissent.
In the opinion of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, this threat will continue so long as intrusive surveillance is permitted on the basis of such shadowy, ethereal and overbroad concepts as "activities directed toward", "ultimate" intentions, and "detrimental" interests. There is supposedly an exemption for activities such as lawful advocacy, protest or dissent. But this is not an adequate definition. It is not clear that activities such as fund raising or commercial negotiations would be included. But some of the activities I just mentioned could be kept out of the exemption section and the group concerned could then come under surveillance by the security service.
There is good reason to question how much additional security is obtained through this level of preventive intelligence gathering. There have been plenty of instances in the United States, and the American Government has moved away from this kind of vague fishing expedition to try and get intelligence from groups engaged in quite lawful dissent. It has simply not come about that any additional security has been obtained from this. Generally, the FBI did not report advance knowledge of planned violence. We really cannot have any hope that by having these Draconian measures we will actually achieve any national security objectives.
Between Bill C-157 and Bill C-9 a few amendments were made but they did not in any significant way increase the protections given, so that the kind of criticism we have been raising still largely holds. These very modest wording changes have not been at all adequate to the task. The NDP has proposed much more substantial amendments. We have passed the stage where we can get them through, but to give you an idea of the kind of constructive alternative we see as appropri-

June 21, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
ate-yes, we do need a civilian security service and it does need to have powers to do things but it must have adequate safeguards. We do have some constructive proposals and we would like to see the Government abandon the Bill as it is now, hold some public hearings and listen to the citizens it has been elected to serve. It can then come back with legislation which would provide adequate protection for the civil liberties we want to have in Canada.
This would mean changes in the definition of threats to the security of Canada. We want to be sure that so-called domestic subversion is not included in this section. The RCMP should continue to have a mandate to deal with domestic subversion according to criminal standards, a procedure which has been used and a distinction which is accepted in the United States. We do not know how serious this threat of domestic subversion is, but we think, in so far as we are going to need it, the ordinary criminal operations of the RCMP with the ordinary standards and safeguards would be the most appropriate way of dealing with these threats.
The criteria for security assessments is another point on which the Bill goes much too far. Too many public servants are subjected to security clearance procedures. In 1982 over
75,000	people were security cleared. It is just very hard to imagine that the threat of spies in the Public Service of Canada is so serious that we need this large number of clearances. The criteria should be spelled out in the Statute or, at the very least, provision made for criteria established by regulation to be made public and subject to review by an oversight committee. The civilian security service should not have responsibility for conducting the security assessments. Their role should be restricted to threats to the security of Canada. Either the RCMP or a branch of the Public Service Commission, as recommended by the McDonald Commission, should have the job.
As to the foreign intelligence function, the Bill would confer new and unprecedented powers on the civilian security service to target individuals who pose no threat to the security of Canada. This could include political refugees, visiting professors and business or labour leaders. This power does not currently exist and there is absolutely no justification for it being included in the legislation.
On the exchange of security information, the Solicitor General has stated that the RCMP security service presently shares information on Canadians with foreign security agencies, including those which do not have proper recognition in their own country. This is a rather dicey procedure at the best of times, but this Bill would codify this practice.
We need a much more adequate review process. The McDonald Commission and many witnesses recommended that there be a Parliamentary oversight committee. Other countries have them. They need full access to Cabinet documents and the information the security service itself has so that it can ensure there have not been violations of civil liberties.
Apart from powers of electronic surveillance and surreptitious entry, as well as the power to make copies of records, there is no justification whatsoever for the expanded powers
sought by the new agency. Even the McDonald Commission recommended that intrusive techniques not be used against domestic subversives. Where we use these intrusive measures, there has to be good reason for it. The threat has to be a serious one. They should not be used on fishing expeditions or for security clearance and things of that sort. The RCMP Commissioner stated that if he were denied access to these intrusive powers, his ability to perform his duties would be impaired only to a "very, very marginal extent". Yet the potential invasion of privacy is incredibly broad. Here we have this threat of far too expensive powers being used even where there are not serious matters of national security.
This Bill would arbitrarily deny collective bargaining rights to virtually all employees of a new service. That is simply inappropriate and unfair. When we compare the safeguards in the U.S. with those here, we see that the Americans and the FBI have far more adequate safeguards. They have to show standards that are similar to ours for criminal investigation, and it gives a far better understanding to the people in this system of what they are legally entitled to do and what they are not.
Our Bill, however, has one merit that the Americans do not have. These safeguards, if we had them, would be legislated. Here we have before us a Bill which would do a desirable thing. It would institute a civilian security service and legislate its powers clearly for all to see, as well as the safeguards. The problem is that what is legislated by way of safeguards is fairly inadequate.
The options before us are quite simple; either to pass the legislation as it is and bring in a new era of substantial abuse of Canadian civil liberties, or we can go slower, the Government can not proceed with the Bill. We have a security service in place. The RCMP are performing that function right now. There is no risk of harm by taking another look to see that we have adequate safeguards.
I see my time is just about up. I want to say that I am very distressed at what we have before us today. It is an interesting point that we see this at the end of the Trudeau period in Government, a piece of legislation that would violate Canadians' civil liberties. We see a former civil libertarian at the end of his parliamentary career bringing in a despicable piece of legislation. It is a sad way for someone to go, and I am sad to see this legislation before us. Last night we had the example-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Chair has been very considerate to the Hon. Member. She has been extended extra time. I have to inform the House that her time has expired. A 10 minute question and comment period is now provided for. Are there any questions or comments. For debate, the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby).

Mr. Speaker, we are now proceeding to the final stage of the deliberations in the House of Commons on Bill C-9 which enacts the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act. It has been a tedious pro-
June 21, 1984

cess, but it has not provided sufficient time in terms of the close examination which ought to be applied to the legislative provisions contained in Bill C-9. The debate is under the strictures and duress of time allocation or closure. Members of the House of Commons are restricted in the amount of time they can devote to the debate on this legislative measure and the provisions of Bill C-9.
It becomes necessary in the final hours of this debate to explain in clear and careful terms what one's position is with respect to this legislation which deals with the security of the citizens of Canada and Canadian institutions. I will explain very carefully my own position. I recognize that there is a potential for threats to security in Canada. I recognize that our democratic society allows a large measure of freedom for its citizens and all residents of Canada, regardless of whether they enjoy the status of citizenship. Within that conglomerate of people there could be those who would harm our society and institutions. The principle of freedom and liberty ought to prevail over all threats, including threats to the security of the nation. That is why this nation was created in the first place. Democracy was established and survives because we believe in freedom. The risk of that belief is that we must recognize that there is the potential in our society for the destruction of our own democratic institutions.
When the predecessor of Bill C-9, Bill C-157, was before the special committee of the Senate, the Senators who dealt with the legislative provisions contained therein recognized the need for that balance between the handling of threats to our society and liberty. They said as a committee that that balance must be maintained. That was the test which governed security legislation. I do not think the members of the Senate committee directed the balance in the right way. That is to say, the members of that committee were prepared to err on the side of protection of society, in the way in which they envisioned that protection, rather than to err on the side of liberty of the subject. The real protection of Canadian society is the liberty of the subject. It is not the laws that are designed by legislators that protect the society. It is the principle of liberty of the subject that protects society.
That principle was established long ago in the mother country of Great Britain. It continues there today, notwithstanding parades to Trafalgar Square and mass movements of labour supporters and ban the bombers which my colleague from Dartmouth-Halifax East has seen on many occasions in the streets of London. Notwithstanding that apparent almost revolutionary attitude, liberty survives in the United Kingdom as it survives nowhere else in the world. If we allow that tradition of liberty to be eroded because of real or alleged threats to Canadian institutions arising from subversion or breaches of security, we may endanger the very society that we are trying to protect.
It is in that context that I want to examine the provisions of Bill C-9 for the last time. We must recognize the need for a balance between the protection of society and the absolute need for civil liberties to be maintained throughout Canada. It is interesting to note that the sponsor of this Bill in the House, 80152-38
Security Intelligence Service
the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) who now sits in his seat, would in most respects be the advocate of civil liberties. In the debate which involves Mr. Sakharov and Mr. Shcharansky I am sure the Solicitor General would be the first to endorse the right of peaceful dissent as a principle of democratic society. I am sure the Solicitor General would be willing to write to the ambassador from the Soviet Union and ask why Mr. Sakharov and Mr. Shcharansky have been treated in the way in which they have been. I am sure he would ask why their liberties are restricted simply because they disagree with the duly constituted, if not elected, government of the Soviet Union.
If we are going to apply the principle of peaceful dissent to citizens of other nations, particularly those which we do not regard as democratic, then we had better be darn sure that we allow for that same kind of peaceful dissent in our own country. Does that make me, or any other Member of the House of Commons who endorses that principle, an advocate of peaceful dissent? Does that colour me as a revolutionary? Does that make me a foe of the system and an enemy of the country? Of course not. I am here to protect the citizens of this country. That is why I examined Bill C-9. I say that it is tipping the balance in the wrong direction and does not recognize, to the extent that it should, the liberty of the subject.
At this stage of the deliberations on Bill C-9 we cannot examine the provisions of the Bill in detail. That was done under the constraint of limited time provided by the closure order imposed by the Government majority. We in the Opposition cannot fight that. All we can do is to explain once again what our position is and what the concern of Canadians ought to be.
I will mention another incident in the House of Commons which dealt with the civil liberties of Canadians. It was passed under the guise of urgency and the need for immediate action. On October 25, 1983 the House of Commons passed Bill C-169 which amended the Canada Elections Act. It made some very useful changes to that Act.
You voted for it.

One of the changes which was made related to advertising during election campaigns. Members of the House who were interested in improving the Canada Elections Act wanted those changes instituted because some of them would be very helpful to the electorate in the important task of choosing its representatives in the Parliament of Canada. We wanted those reforms to take place. However, not all Members were aware that an amendment to Section 70.1 might have the effect of outlawing legitimate protests in the form of election period advertising. No one was aware of that. The haste with which Bill C-169 was passed by the House of Commons caused difficulty and concern among a great many Canadians about this intrusion on their liberty by the elimination of their right of free expression. The haste was responsible for that.
Let me make it clear that all Members of the House of Commons have to bear the responsibility for that. We created

June 21, 1984

the haste and allowed it to exist. We allowed it to be carried out and did not fight it. We went along with it because we wanted those reforms. Now we have the result. We cannot now get the co-operation of the Government to make changes to rectify the error that may have been made by the House of Commons in passing Bill C-169. We are not able to say that we made a mistake in not realizing that the provision had that effect. Had we realized that, we would not have participated in a unanimous endorsement of Bill C-169. The Government says no, it is sorry, we made a mistake but the provision is there and it will be applied. The Government says, "We will tell the people of Canada that they cannot advertise during an election campaign in the way that it is now alleged to be prohibited by the statutory provision". It says that we made the mistake and the people of Canada will pay for it.
That is what will happen with Bill C-9. If there are any mistakes made by the House of Commons, the people of Canada will pay for them. That is why we must stand here and protest the provisions of the Bill. That is why we must stand up and tell the Government to give us more time because there may be provisions in the Bill that will cause grave concern to the people of Canada.
Remember Revenue Canada. Whoever looked at legislation governing Revenue Canada to find out that it could have secret forces examining the habits of people in Canada in order to determine whether it might affect the manner in which they pay their income tax? Who would have thought that when an institution like Statistics Canada was created, a legitimate institution to compile statistics, that they would be out running around asking people about their income and demanding that they fill out forms that make inquiries ranging from their sex life to their financial demands?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Like calling Richardsons to ask for files.

Anything in the name of statistics. That is not what the Parliament of Canada intended for Statistics Canada. It was not creating a snoop service to create statistics that nobody needs or finds useful. Yet there are employees of Statistics Canada this very day throughout the country who are knocking on doors and demanding that people fill out forms that those citizens quite sincerely believe this action is an instrusion on their privacy and their right as Canadians citizens to live the way they want without violation of any law. Those government employees are invoking a law against those citizens which was never intended to be invoked and applied in that way.
It is the fault of Members of Parliament for not building a mechanism into the system which would prevent that kind of action. Who ever thought in the House of Commons, when the concept of social insurance numbers was introduced, that they would be used as an intelligence gathering technique? Who ever thought that one's SIN number was going to be used to find our whether one paid one's Visa bill or the Royal Bank of Canada. Who ever thought these things would happen?
Not only should we be on guard for these kinds of changes, we have an absolute duty to be on guard and make sure that any such changes or anything that involves the liberty of the subject in Canada has to be carefully scrutinized or we will end up with Sakharovs and Shcharanskys in Canada, and it will be the Russians asking how we are treating our citizens and why are we snooping around asking where their bank accounts are and how much is in them. I wonder if they do that in the Soviet Union? I wonder if they knock on doors and ask those questions.
We can be ashamed of some of the things going on in Canada because they do not need to take place. We do not need that kind of activity because this is a democratic country. Perhaps there is an element of subversion and threat to our security. We do not deny that. However, it is not necessary to use an elephant gun to kill an ant and that is what the Solicitor General is doing.
Incidentally, what does he know about these situations? He has been harboured away in the middle of the City of Toronto all of his life. What does he know about threats to our society? What information has he received and what information is he relying on?
I have lived in this country. I have served in the administration of justice for a number of years. I never saw any great threats to our society that required the urgent passage of legislation in the Parliament of Canada creating the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. It is not required on an urgent basis so that the rules must be stopped and the process must be stopped in order to get it passed. That is nonsense and the Solicitor General should know that.
If he thinks that the people of Canada agree with him and not with what I am saying he is wrong, because there are very ordinary people in Canada who write very ordinary letters to Members of Parliament to say things such as, "I have just finished reading an article in the paper stating that the Conservative caucus proposes to maintain the RCMP security service as is. I wholeheartedly support this idea". This person happens to be a member of the Canadian Armed Forces. He goes on to give some very cogent reasons for maintaining the RCMP as an intelligence service.
A woman who is in business in my constituency wrote me asking to maintain the RCMP and not to establish a civilian security agency. She knows what government agencies are like and what their track record is. She knows what will happen. She has dealt with Statistics Canada. She runs a business and knows what Revenue Canada is like when it comes to forms, details and records. Are we to believe that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service will be any different? Are we to believe it will be any better than Revenue Canada or more considerable than Statistics Canada in getting reports? Not on your life.
I'll bet that within six months the Inspector General of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service will have a uniform with more gold braid on it than any admiral ever thought of having. I will bet that it will have everyone institutionalized and militarilized in a matter of months. The Solicitor General
June 21, 1984

had better not laugh. Has he not seen his correctional officers prancing around the country with their gold braided hats. Is not the Canadian Correctional Service a civilian service? What are they doing in uniforms and why are they marching? Its a potential disease. It is called fascism.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You know it.
The Solicitor General should certainly know what the results of that disease can be if it is not stopped.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: If you don't, 15 years down the road you will wake up one morning and wonder why it happened.

We want to balance rights and we want to balance it in all types of legislation. But we want to do it particularly with legislation that deals with civil rights and the liberty of the subject in Canada.
Let me talk about the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in that situation. The Royal Mounted Police is a national institution that was created in 1873. It has 110 years of history in Canada. What has happened? This is the report of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police included in the Solicitor General's own report. According to that report, its mandate is to enforce Canadian laws, prevent crime, maintain peace, order and security.
When we examined this report we found with respect to airports that the RCMP ticketed 250,000 cars. That is to say, they issued 250,000 tickets to Canadians at airports. The RCMP has been allowed to degenerate as a police service in Canada. They are not the same as they were in 1873, there is no doubt about that.
This will just be another blow to the RCMP. I do not care what Commissioner Simmonds says about that. He is not on the streets. He is not in Sackville, Nova Scotia, or out in British Columbia. He does not chase after Olson and those kinds of people. He does not know how the ability of the RCMP to perform normal police tasks has been destroyed.
I would like to hear from the Solicitor General on the subject of drugs. They talked about drugs and drug activity. They estimate the value of drugs with which they were involved in 1981 at $8 billion. They say that is the value of the drug market in Canada and that it may be exaggerated. It is in this report. Eight billion dollars is total nonsense. In 1981, that was more than 15 per cent of the total revenues of the Government of Canada, yet they say that is what is out on the streets of Canada. What streets of Canada? I have travelled all over Canada and while there is a serious drug problem which must be attacked, do not tell me that there is $8 billion floating around Canada in the drug market.
It is those kinds of activities in which the RCMP are involved. They are not providing the basic police service that they ought to provide. The Canadian Security Intelligence Service will be taking that much more away from the RCMP and leaving them in parking lots at airports ticketing cars and
Security Intelligence Service
leaving them out on the streets chasing impaired drivers or speeders, when they should be chasing rapists, murderers and people who break and enter private dwellings.
It is not the history or the employees that is hurting the RCMP, it is the direction it is getting from the top. Members of the RCMP who endorse a transferring of security services to a so-called civilian from the RCMP are not contributing to the future welfare and well-being of the RCMP. That force has been in existence for a long time. It does not belong to the officers at the top of that organization. It does not belong to the Solicitor General. It belongs to all Canadians. It is a Canadian force created by Canadians. It is an institution in Canada.
The RCMP is now responsible to the government-to the Solicitor General. He does not have the right to take any act that is going to hurt that force as a Canadian institution, but that is what the Government is doing with Bill C-9. It is taking action that will be harmful to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a Canadian institution, and harmful to Canadians, mark my words, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: For debate, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer).

I have spoken several times on this important bit of legislation, Mr. Speaker, and I make no apologies for that. I think every Member of this House should be on his or her feet opposing this legislation. I think they should be on their feet as often as is necessary to get this Government to change this very flawed legislation. Certainly I do not think I have seen a more important Bill come before this House of Commons. It directly affects the rights, the privacy, and the freedoms of every individual Canadian in this country. I think the Opposition has an obligation to effect changes in this legislation.
We in the Opposition recognize the need for a security force in Canada, but we are not prepared to approve of or respond to legislation which makes that force or gives it the right seriously to hamper the freedoms of Canadians and seriously intrude on their private lives. Unfortunately, the Government has seen fit to exercise closure on this Bill. It has used the guillotine of time allocation to ensure that the Government gets the Bill through the House before the end of the session. I cannot understand why the Government is doing that, Mr. Speaker. Certainly there does not seem to be any reason for this unseemly haste. I can assure you, Sir, that what this Government does in haste with respect to this legislation, the people of Canada will repent at leisure. As sure as I am standing here, this Bill will lead to great injustice to Canadians over the next few years.

June 21, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
The Canadian Catholic Conference has called upon the Government to have a sober second look at the legislation. Many organizations, in fact every organization that appeared before the committee asked for changes in the legislation and told the Government to slow down and take a good look at it.
Let us see who made appearances before the committee. Here are just a few: The Canadian Medical Association, the Attorneys General of Canada, the Voice of Women, the Civil Liberties Associations from most provinces, trade unions, from across Canada both large and small, the Association of University Professors, ethnic groups who are really concerned about what this legislation will do to their organizations and the Canadian Council of Churches. There were many, many others, not the least of which was the Canadian Bar Association. All these groups had valid complaints in areas of concern to them.
I think one of the most penetrating comments I have heard in relation to this legislation was that made by Bishop De Roo of Victoria, the President of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. Bishop De Roo wrote a letter to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) with a copy sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In part, this is what Bishop De Roo wrote:
The content of the Bill worries us considerably. Its adoption without major amendments could very well indicate that Canada is not afraid when it comes to introducing repressive measures aimed at attacking civil and political liberties in order to control social unrest provoked by the application of restraint policies.
Bishop De Roo has got to the heart of one of the problems in this legislation, and certainly this Government cannot claim a good record in that regard. We have only to look at the imposition of the War Measures Act to see how quickly this Government would respond to a farce, and how quickly it would depress civil liberties on some bogey men appearing. That is exactly what this legislation is in great danger of doing.
I am worried, members of my Party are worried and the Canadian people are very worried about this legislation.
Hear, hear!

The record will show that the changes proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party to this legislation are generally supported by the groups I have mentioned, indeed generally supported by all Canadians. I think the changes in the legislation that we have put forward have been prompted in the main by the response of Canadians to the establishment through this legislation of a security force.
I want to put on the record tonight, although I have mentioned it before, as have other people, the main changes we have requested. I think this Bill will get Canadians into a lot of trouble and we should be able to look back historically and find out where the trouble started.
First, we have proposed three main areas of change. When I say three main areas, I am not including all of the amendments that were put forward, some of them very important, but I do not have the time tonight to go through them all. I would like to go through the ones I consider most important.
First, we propose that the new security force stay within the RCMP. You might well wonder why, Mr. Speaker. I think it is very clear. This is new legislation. It creates a distinctive secret service security force of which Canadians instinctively are suspicious. I say that particular about western Canadians. They are very worried about the establishment of this kind of thing. Frankly, in western Canada we have not had too much good come out of Ottawa. We look with a jaundiced eye on any kind of legislation, and we look at a fearful eye on any establishment of more security forces. Therefore, it is most important to overcome that fear; some of which may be justified, parts of it not. Why not keep the force within the RCMP which is a highly respected and successful force? All over Canada and all over the world the RCMP has earned recognition and respect. Its members are trained to respect the law in Canada. That is why they have had the confidence of the people.
We have had a security force in this country for a long time. And the Attorney General, in response to questions at the committee, admitted that the RCMP had done a very good job, that there are no complaints, that the RCMP has successfully used all the methods necessary and it has developed a highly successful security force.
The question is, if you have a successful operation, why change it? We have pushed very hard to have the Government accept the idea of the security force remaining with the RCMP.
Let me be the first to point out that that was not essential to our position. I am sure we would not have had this long debate if the Government had made some other changes and said that it would keep the force or make a new force. I think we could live with that, reluctantly, but we could live with it. Certainly most of the Attorneys General of Canada support the force being within the RCMP as did the Civil Liberties Association of British Columbia who are not inclined to put the RCMP on a pedestal. That association indicated that if we must have this legislation, it should be left with the RCMP. However, that is not the main issue. The main issue is the definitions contained in Clause 2. I think most Hon. Members have spoken to that particular clause and its horrendous definitions.
We in the Progressive Conservative Party have taken the position throughout this whole matter that if we are to have legislation creating a security force, it is absolutely essential to define the limits of its activities. Without that, a legislative sanction is given to a large group of people without any restraints whatsoever. Clause 2 has been badly drafted and provides no protection at all. In fact, it allows the security force to conduct activities which the Government did not intend.
In the time remaining I should like to point out the dangers. In part, Clause 2 reads:
"threats to the security of Canada" means
June 21, 1984

(a)	espionage or sabotage that is against Canada or is detrimental to the interests of Canada or activities directed toward or in support of such espionage or sabotage,
However, the word "sabotage" is not defined. The dictionary defines that word as wanton destruction of equipment. That kind of thing happens frequently in Canada. I could point to industrial and labour disputes where machinery gets damaged. Surely it is not the intention of the Government to have the secret police investigate industrial and labour disputes, yet that definition allows them to do so. It is just one example of many loose and poor definitions.
The clause continues:
(b)	foreign influenced activities within or relating to Canada that are detrimental to the interests of Canada and are clandestine or deceptive or involve a threat to any person,
Let us examine that closely. It could mean that the director of this super-snooper force could begin an intrusive investigation of Japanese automobile dealers in Canada meeting in secret to determine their pricing policy. That is exactly what it could mean, but surely that is not what the Government intended. It has admitted that it did not intend that, yet it is allowing the secret service force to have the ability to participate in wide-ranging activities. Any time any force is given limits to their activities they tend to use them to the limit, and we are lucky if they do not exceed them. I have yet to see this proven otherwise.
If a citizen met discreetly and quietly with Chilean exiles opposed to the Pinochet regime with which Canada has domestic industrial relations, he or she could be in trouble. I could continue listing a number of examples. I think this situation is very dangerous and that it should be looked at carefully. Before this evening is over perhaps the Government will change its mind. If it does not, it should be warned that the people of Canada will not change their minds and they will have their retribution at election time.
I should like to continue referring to Clause 2. I have not reached the worst part as yet. It continues:
(c)	activities within or relating to Canada directed toward or in support of the threat or use of acts of serious violence against person or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state,-
This means that the security force might investigate, and probably would investigate anyone who attended an Israel bond drive dinner or anyone who supported the PLO organization in Canada or the rebels in Afghanistan. Who knows? They could be under investigation by the force. Surely the Government did not mean to have the activities of such people investigated. Perhaps it did, but I cannot believe that. What possible excuse could the Government have for including such a wide definition?
Now I should like to turn to what is probably the worst definition of all. It should not even be in the Act. It reads:
(d)	activities directed toward undermining by covert unlawful acts, or directed toward or intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow by violence of, the constitutionally established system of government in Canada,
This goes to the fundamental right of Canadians to protest or dissent. It goes to the heart of the democratic system. It is a
Security Intelligence Service
very delicate subject, I am quite aware of that. However, I should like to read into the record what John Starnes said, as reported in the June 18 edition of the Weekend Observer. I think he dealt with the point very well when he said:
The definition of politically motivated violence has been widened so that those engaging in relatively unimportant acts of political violence can become targets of the service.
The Bill defines subversion as "activities ... directed toward or intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow of the constitutionally established system of government in Canada." The McDonald Commission proposed the phrase, "the democratic system of government in Canada." A small but important distinction.
Presumably the definition in the Bill means the service, using all the means at its disposal, could investigate activities aimed at the separation of a province.
He went on to say that if the Government intended to resort to this kind of thing, it should make it very well known. That is exactly what this definition allows the service to do. Is it any wonder that the Government of Quebec is so upset by this piece of legislation?
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Is the Hon. Member referring to the amended Bill which contains the word "by violence"? I am not sure whether his quotation made reference to those two words.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is not a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I agree that that is not a point of order. However, I am not referring to the old legislation. I am referring to the new one. I am well aware of the differences.
Be that as it may, this clause will be opposed. There are many separatist organizations out west. They are sincere in what they mean. They are running around rose-bushes and things of that nature. I do not agree with them, but I certainly agree with their right to exist. Just because of their political philosophy, they should not be investigated by a security service. In that regard this is the worst legislation we have ever had in the country. Our citizens certainly do not need political dissent triggering intrusive investigations. That is the one thing we do not need.
The definitions are far too broad. If anything in the Act is bad, it is Clause 2. The entire Bill could be cleaned up in a few areas. The Government could readily do this. I know the Government will say in reply that it has done so, but if we look at the last paragraph in Clause 2, it reads: but does not include lawful advocacy, protest or dissent,-
Then it continues:
-unless carried on in conjunction with any of the activities referred to in paragraphs (a) to paragraph (d).
In other words, the Government does not want to exclude anything. That is the meanest bit of doubletake in draftsmanship I have ever seen.
I understand that I have a minute remaining. I plead once more with the Government to withdraw the Bill or to accept some changes so that it could at least be more acceptable to Canadians.

June 21, 1984
Security Intelligence Service

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a few questions to my colleague. First of all, I sincerely hope that, after the intervention of my colleague from Laurier (Mr. Berger), he did not mean to imply that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service would be unable to investigate, should any kind of organization seek to undermine Canada's constitutional regime through violent means. I do hope that is not what he meant, because that would pave the way for anarchists in Canada. I wish he would comment on that first part.
The other thing which has me worried is that it is somewhat difficult to find out just where the Progressive Conservative Party stands with respect to the creation of a civilian intelligence agency. The House knows the position of the Canadian Government: in light of the Mackenzie, McDonald and Pit-field reports, it proposes the creation of a civilian security intelligence service independent from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Then we have the New Democratic Party which is openly against the RCMP and its alleged activities and which, in the same breath, wants the RCMP to continue to work in the field of intelligence security. And then, the Progressive Conservative Party, which brings me to this question: can anyone tell us in clear, unequivocal and specific terms just what the position of the Progressive Conservative Party is?
In committee, it sounded as if they were against the creation of a civilian security intelligence agency, and yet four Progressive Conservative senators sat on the Pitfield committee and only one was against the creation of a civilian security intelligence agency.
What I would like to know is, what is the exact position of the Progressive Conservative Party, and what is the position of the Members of the Progressive Conservative caucus? Does their position differ from that of the caucus of senators, if indeed there is such a thing? And how can we reconcile the position expressed by the Progressive Conservative Party critic of the Solicitor General with the statements made by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who tends to favour the creation of a civilian security intelligence agency?

I think that answers the question. Is that what the Hon. Member wanted clarified?

what they can do. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Okanagan North can indicate whether his Party is going to stick to its principles and to its guns and do what it can in the Senate to block this Bill, or is it going to let it slide through in the Senate?

Mr. Speaker, as we debate the last stage of Bill C-9 I cannot escape the sense of sadness and melancholy that I feel. After sitting and voting until five o'clock this morning, I think the nerves of all of us are frayed and we feel physically and emotionally exhausted. I believe that is true for all Members of the House.
Despite all of the efforts displayed by the combined Opposition, the Government has refused to budge. We have used almost every instrument that is available to an Opposition to impress upon the Government our fears and uncertainties about the security legislation. The Government has refused to consider seriously any and all of our representations.
Security Intelligence Service
Members of the two opposition Parties do not oppose this legislation because we wish to score some political points or play some political games. We have a very genuine fear that the secret service agency to be established by this Bill will pose serious threats to the civil liberties of Canadians and hamper genuine and legitimate dissent. We are not alone in our fears. Church groups, the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, and all of the provincial Attorneys General share our fears. Yet the Government continues to ignore these very real fears. It abuses it majority by blocking amendments, by imposing closure and by ramming this Bill through the House.
I am still genuinely puzzled why the Government insists it needs such wide powers over the lives of individual Canadians. Government Members, and particularly the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), have not proven that a state of anarchy or insurrection exists in Canada. They have not shown that a threat exists with which the Government does not already have the means to deal. Why when does it need a secret police service with more powers than any other police force that exists in any democratic country? Are there greater threats being made by terrorists or subversives in Canada than in the United States, Italy, Germany or Great Britain? Certainly the Government has not even attempted to prove that this is so. Why then is the Government so insistent on getting this legislation through the House without any amendments?
Some Liberal Members have stated that Bill C-9 is what the McDonald Commission recommended. However, that is entirely false. Government Members have claimed that this Bill will rectify the injustices and illegal acts that were committed during the Quebec crisis. Sadly, I find this argument to be an example of Orwellian doublespeak. It was this Liberal Government that imposed the War Measures Act and that determined the manner in which it would deal with the FLQ threat. History has now shown that the Liberal Government overreacted. To absolve themselves of their collective guilt, Liberal Members have attempted to make the RCMP the scapegoat, and they have used the McDonald Commission report as an excuse to make legal all of the illegal acts that occurred. It is cynical, it is Orwellian, and it is repugnant to reasonable men and women.
I am still at a very genuine loss to understand why the Government wants this legislation so badly now. Perhaps some time in the future we will discover the real reason why this is so. We cannot accept the half-baked arguments that government Members have proposed as justification for this legislation. There is another reason for this, which we do not know. Another reason exists in the background of which Canadians are not aware. Hopefully, at some point in history, the complete truth will be known why the Government wanted this legislation so desperately at this time.
Why have we been so adamant in our opposition to this Bill? First, as many Members on this side of the House have indicated, and as others who have brought forward briefs and presentations have also indicated, the definitions in the Bill are much too loose. For example, the definition of what constitutes

June 21, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
a threat to the security of Canada is so loosely worded that all sorts of very legitimate political organizations and activities can be considered a threat to Canadian security. On the domestic front it could mean that unemployed workers who are involved in demonstrations, farmers who are going into bankruptcy and using tractors in demonstrations, and peace groups and activists involved in peace marches and in collecting petitions, could all be defined as a threat to the security of Canada.
We are not saying that those groups will be defined in such a way, but we are saying that there are enough holes in this proposed legislation that one individual person obsessed with his notion of the nature of Canadian society could decide that these farm groups, work groups, and peace groups constitute a threat to Canadian society. As such, the people involved in those organizations can have their telephones tapped, their medical records and taxation records looked into, their homes broken into at any time of the night, and they can essentially lose their basic civil liberties as Canadian citizens.
The second reason why we are so afraid of this piece of legislation is the nature of the powers it gives to this agency. The powers are much too wide. They are frightening. They are repugnant to Canadian traditions and to the Canadian way of life. For the Government even to dare to enter Parliament with a type of legislation that gives these powers to a group of men and women should be an unthinkable act. Yet this Government has, in the dying days of this Parliament, done just that.
The third area with which we are concerned is the area of accountability. If we need a secret service agency with wide powers, then at least we must do everything possible to make certain that that agency has some accountability. If we are at all concerned that this agency does not get away with itself, then we must put in place a method of checks and balances so that this agency can be accountable and so that the men and women who are in charge of this agency are accountable to people outside the agency. The accountability provided for by this legislation is much too weak, and in fact, hardly exists at all.
Government Members will, of course, say that this agency cannot get away with itself. We cannot accept that argument. There are too many examples of bureaucracies under this Liberal regime running away with themselves. The most recent and glaring example of this is, of course, the recent controversy surrounding Revenue Canada. It is a Department which has no real policing powers or policing mandate, yet it created an entire internal police network that rode roughshod over individual civil liberties of the Canadian people.
We are very much afraid that this security agency can run away with itself in the same fashion. We are very much concerned that a secret police bureaucracy can be created that will no longer be held accountable to its political masters. The history of the Liberal Government in this country should be a fair warning to all of us that this indeed can happen.
Administratively the Liberals have shown themselves to be quite incompetent. They cannot even hold their own bureaucracy in check. How well can the present Solicitor General, with his great brilliance, be able to hold in check the monster he is creating? I have a personal admiration and respect for the Solicitor General as a human being, but I have no confidence in the Solicitor General having the smarts to be able to control the secret service agency which he is creating. In fact I would suggest that he is the very opposite-relatively incompetent on that matter.
We have challenged the Government to hold an election on this issue. We have told the Government that if this is such an important item it should come out of the closet, go public and tell the Canadian people exactly why we need this agency and why these policing powers are necessary. What threats exist to the security and well-being of the people of Canada? Of course government Members react to that suggestion by laughing at us.
Going through the process of the debate on this legislation at second reading, and now third reading, the one area which I find particularly saddening is the lack of media attention and concern about this Bill. Surely it is the duty of the media to inform Canadians on all matters which directly affect them. Surely the legislation with which we are dealing today has tremendous impact on the fundamental freedoms of Canadians.
The debate on this Bill should have been front-page news. All of the arguments should have been reported, pro and con. Had we had more attentive media and had the media insisted that the debate on this Bill be a high item on the social agenda that Canadians would read and talk about, the Government would have accepted more amendments. Had the media played their role, the Government would never have been allowed to get away with introducing closure. In fact, had there been an attentive media, more Liberal Members of Parliament would have stood to justify the legislation. Unfortunately, the media have not played their true and important role in this matter.
In a very few days this Bill will receive Royal Assent and it will be law. We can only hope and pray that the men and women who will have unprecedented powers over their fellow Canadians will use those powers judiciously and wisely. I hope that they will not cynically dismiss the fears and concerns of the churches, the provincial Attorneys General, and the civil liberties unions, as just the outpouring of a bunch of touchies and feelies. I hope these men and women will not ignore what members of the Opposition in the House of Commons have been saying. After all, we are the representatives of the people. I fervently hope that these men and women do not become consumed by their own visions of what Canadian society should be, and that will not be allowed to harass and intrude into the private lives of Canadians whose visions are different from theirs.
We face a very uncertain future. It is a future of tremendous technological changes. Many of these technological changes will endanger the private rights and security of Canadians.
June 21, 1984

The computerization of medical and legal files, electronic banking, border transfer of data, and some of the most sophisticated electronic devices to listen to conversations, are readily available on the market today. All these new devices and all these new social institutions will restrict individual privacy. We expected legislation which would protect individual Canadians rather than legislation which will help to facilitate the invasion of the privacy of individual Canadians.
As Canadian society moves into the future, it will encounter different social and economic changes and upheavals. Some individuals will be displaced. Today we see hundreds and thousands of men and women who are not able to find work. In today's Globe and Mail there was an article about the slave trade in Calgary. Men gather in a block area, and people drive by in trucks and vans to pick up unemployed men and hire them as labourers for a day. Those men do not have any protection in terms of working conditions or minimum wage standards.
Every day in the City of Vancouver there are four or five block-long line-ups of young Canadian men and women who are waiting to get a sandwich because that is- their only source of food. Indeed, these are difficult times for many Canadians. These are times in which it is inevitable that some will get angry at the conditions in which they have to live their lives. For these people to have a secret service agency on top of that, will drive some of them underground. I predict that the existence of a secret service agency will create the opposite effect than what was intended by this Bill. It will create more subversives. It is like a mirror image-the one creates the other. When Canadians fear that they can no longer advocate the changing of the conditions in which they and their fellow citizens must live, and that they are afraid that a secret service agency will spy on them because they are advocating some change in the power and in the economic structure of this country, then they will feel that they must go underground. The one does create the other.
As we move into a very insecure future, this piece of legislation will not help us to find a new and just future for Canadian men and women. It will have the opposite effect. It is a sad day for this Parliament. This great democratic institution will pass into law a Bill which limits and restricts democracy. Democracy is the most fragile of flowers. The experience of men and women in the history of our democratic race is a very recent experience. It is a very fragile flower indeed, which is being attacked by changing conditions as we move into the future. I am afraid that what the Government has proposed and what it is asking us to pass in this session is a Bill which will help destroy that flower. In the name of attempting to protect it, the very mechanism which it is creating to protect democracy becomes a threat to democracy. The Government has been unwilling to listen to us and to take seriously our fears and representations. It has been adamant in pushing this Bill through the House. I must return to the question-Why?

speechtext:
Questions or comments, Mr. Speaker. Earlier, the Hon. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada

I very well remember the mayor who was there. He represented a community of mayors, somewhat like municipal regions we have in our Quebec constituencies.
I would like to know, from the Hon. Member who spoke of the problems that might stem from the establishment of a new Security Information agency, whether he is fully aware of the review and control process in the Canadian Security Intelligence Agency. Did he inform the people correctly, referring to the review by the judicial process, by the Minister, by the Inspector General, by the Review Committee, whose Members are appointed in consultation with the Leader of the Official Opposition and the leader of any party holding at least 12 seats in this House? Mr. Speaker, I have informed my constituents that the Government is afraid to have this agency reviewed by their representatives.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
